Four days of frozen politeness in their Kolkata flat, and then, on Saturday morning, Vaibhav put two cups of tea on the table and sat down across from Bidisha.
"Can I explain something?" he said. His hands were around the cup. "When we fight and I go quiet, it's not that I don't care. I get flooded. My head fills up and I'm scared I'll say something cruel."
Bidisha didn't answer at once. She had spent four days thinking the silence was aimed at her.
"So next time," Vaibhav went on, "can I say, 'I need twenty minutes,' and then come back and finish it? I will come back."
Bidisha breathed out. "If you tell me that, I can wait."

qa.a: Four days.

qa.q: What was Vaibhav feeling as he explained, hands around the cup?
qa.a: He seemed nervous and vulnerable, admitting he gets flooded and is scared of saying something cruel.

qa.q: Why was Vaibhav's explanation a turning point?
qa.a: By explaining that he goes quiet when flooded, not because he doesn't care, and asking for a short break with a promised return, he turned silence from a weapon into a signal.

qa.q: What is Bidisha experiencing when she breathes out?
qa.a: She feels relieved and more willing to wait, because now she understands what his silence means.

grounding: A young husband breaks the ice by explaining that he goes quiet when overwhelmed, not from not caring, and asks for a short break with a promised return.

People ask me and Manjula how we fight now. I'm Ritu. We've lived together four years, and the first two were full of silent days.
So we made two rules, and we wrote them on the fridge.
Rule one: you're allowed to pause. But you have to say when you'll come back. "I need till after dinner." "Give me an hour." No open-ended silence.
Rule two: nobody gets left guessing. If you're upset, you say so, even if you can't say why yet.
And we agreed on one more thing: if either of us ever starts using silence to control the other, again and again, we go and see a counsellor. No shame in it. That's what it's for.

qa.q: Where did Ritu and Manjula write their rules?
qa.a: On the fridge.

qa.q: What does Ritu seem to feel now about how they handle conflict?
qa.a: Ritu seems relieved and confident, proud of the rules that replaced their silent days.

qa.q: What makes their new rules work?
qa.a: Pauses are allowed only with a return time, and no one is left guessing, so silence becomes a signal rather than a weapon.

qa.q: How might Manjula experience a pause under the new rules?
qa.a: Manjula can wait calmly, knowing exactly when Ritu will come back, instead of fearing being shut out.

grounding: A young adult describes new rules: pauses allowed with a return time, no one left guessing, and a counsellor if silence becomes controlling.

Can I tell you something I'm not proud of? I'm Baljeet, and last month I did something really stupid.
Kishore's birthday was on Saturday. I'd said yes weeks ago. His mum even calls me her second son. Then on Friday, some seniors invited me to a concert, with passes. I texted Kishore, "Bro, something came up, sorry, will make it up." And I went.
On Sunday I saw his reply: "Cool. Hope it was worth it."
That hit me in the stomach. I felt awful. I knew he'd planned it for weeks.
But part of me was already arguing back. It was just one party. He'd have done the same. It was a concert, man.
I just sat there, holding the phone, feeling both things at once.

qa.a: He is probably hurt and disappointed, feeling that Baljeet chose something better over his birthday.

Sudha, beta, you think your grandfather was always a good friend? Listen. I, Divyansh, at twenty, did a foolish thing.
My friend Ramnath had invited me to his birthday. A small dinner at his mother's house. But the same evening, a rich classmate invited me to his farmhouse. I sent Ramnath a message through his brother: "Something urgent, can't come."
The next day, Ramnath's brother brought me a reply: "Hope your urgent thing was fun."
My face burned. I knew I had hurt him. And yet, part of me thought: it's just a dinner, he'll get over it. I carried both those feelings for days.

grounding: A grandfather recalls cancelling on a friend's birthday for a better invitation at twenty, then feeling guilt mixed with a wish to defend himself.

"Read this," said Omkar, pushing his phone across to Shankar in the hostel room. "Is it okay?"
Shankar read aloud: "'Hey Nandini, I'm sorry if you felt bad about Saturday. The traffic was insane and then work stuff came up. You know how it is.'" He looked up. "You missed her exhibition."
"I know. That's why I'm apologising."
"You're not, though. 'Sorry if you felt' means sorry she's upset, not sorry you didn't show up."
"But there was traffic!"
"For three hours?"
Omkar grabbed his phone back. "I just want this to be over."
"She'll hear that," said Shankar.

qa.q: What did Omkar miss on Saturday?
qa.a: Nandini's exhibition.

qa.q: What was Omkar feeling as he wrote the draft?
qa.a: He felt uncomfortable and defensive, wanting to be forgiven quickly without admitting he was wrong.

qa.q: What turning point does Shankar offer?
qa.a: Shankar points out that "sorry if you felt" is not a real apology, giving Omkar a chance to own that he didn't show up instead of blaming traffic.

qa.q: How might Nandini experience Omkar's draft if he sends it?
qa.a: She would likely feel more hurt, hearing excuses and blame rather than a real apology.

grounding: A young man drafts an apology that begins "sorry if you felt" and blames traffic, wanting forgiveness without the discomfort of being wrong.

I remember the draft I wrote to Jaya after missing her graduation dinner.
It went like this: "Hey, sorry if you felt let down. Work was crazy, my manager kept me back, and then the metro was jammed. Hope you understand."
I read it and felt better. It wasn't my fault, the message said. It was work, the manager, the metro.
Then I read it again, pretending I was Jaya. It didn't say I was sorry for anything. It said I was sorry she felt something. I'd left the office at seven, and the dinner was at eight. The metro wasn't the reason.
I'm Pradeep, and I deleted that message. I didn't want to feel wrong. But I was.

qa.q: What event did Pradeep miss?
qa.a: Jaya's graduation dinner.

qa.q: What was Pradeep feeling when he first read his draft?
qa.a: Pradeep felt better, relieved, because the message put the blame on work, the manager and the metro.

qa.q: What turning point did Pradeep reach?
qa.a: By reading the draft as if Pradeep were Jaya, the excuses became visible, and deleting it opened the way to a real apology.

qa.q: How would Jaya likely have felt reading the original draft?
qa.a: She would probably have felt more hurt and dismissed, reading excuses instead of a real apology.

grounding: A young adult recalls drafting a "sorry if you felt" apology full of excuses, then seeing it as a way to avoid feeling wrong.

Internship supervisor's note, Friday

Tushar came to my desk at lunch and asked me to check an email he'd written to his friend Aadhya. He said it was "important to get it right."
The draft began: "I'm sorry if you felt hurt that I missed your recital. The workload here has been really heavy, and traffic was terrible." He'd missed it on Wednesday.
I asked him, "Did you miss it because of traffic?" He paused. "Not really. I forgot."
I suggested that the email might land better if it said just that: that he forgot, and he's sorry. He looked uncomfortable. He said he'd think about it. I'll check in with him on Monday.

qa.a: Aadhya's recital, on Wednesday.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when the supervisor suggested a simpler email?
qa.a: He seemed uncomfortable, not wanting to feel the discomfort of being wrong.

qa.a: By asking whether traffic was the real reason, the supervisor helped Tushar see the excuses and suggested an honest apology instead.

qa.q: How might Aadhya experience an honest email saying he forgot?
qa.a: She might still feel hurt, but she would likely feel more respected than if she read excuses about traffic.
